source_text: Esau enim profanus et fornicator, propter unam escam vendens primitiva sua, quaesivit benedictionem quam spreverat, nec adeptus est, quamquam eam cum lacrymis poposcisset. Iacob autem quietus et mitis, oboediens parentum praeceptis, et sanctificationum appetentissimus, ad hoc usque provectus est, ut sicut Abrahae et Isaac, ita etiam et Iacob Deus in sancto populo diceretur [n344] . Cum igitur omnibus constaret exemplis, Deum iusto iudicio bonis mentibus in quacumque gente suam misericordiam non negare, malas vero mentes nulla sinere stirpis nobilitate defendi; intellegerent Iudaei Gentium fidem a se despici non debere; quia sicut non patrocinatur Israelitarum stemma criminibus, ita etiam nullo impedimento est Gentium origo virtutibus. Hoc ergo totum agens conflictu illo Apostolus; in quibusdam tamen locis, ad incurvandam circumcisorum arrogantiam, sub nomine gratiae de sola Dei praeiudicat potestate.
pass_a_gloss: For Esau profane and a fornicator, selling his first things on account of one food, sought the blessing which he had spurned, nor obtained it, although he had asked it with tears. But Jacob quiet and mild, obeying the precepts of parents, and most appetent of sanctifications, was advanced to this point, that as of Abraham and Isaac, so also of Jacob God would be said in the holy people. Since therefore it stood by all examples, that God by a just judgment does not deny his mercy to good minds in whatever nation, but allows evil minds to be defended by no nobility of stock; the Jews would understand that the faith of the Nations ought not to be despised by them; because as the stem of Israelites does not patronize crimes, so also the origin of the Nations is no impediment to virtues. The Apostle therefore driving this whole by that conflict; in certain places nevertheless, toward bending the arrogance of the circumcised, under the name of grace he prejudges from the power of God alone.

pass_b_english: For Esau, profane and sexually immoral, sold his birthright for a single meal. He sought the blessing he had despised and did not obtain it, although he begged for it with tears (Hebrews 12:16–17; Genesis 25:29–34; Genesis 27:34–38). Jacob, however, quiet and gentle, obedient to his parents' instructions and most eager for holy blessings, advanced so far that among the holy people God was called the God of Jacob as well as of Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 25:27; Genesis 27:8; Exodus 3:6; Matthew 22:32).

All examples therefore establish that by a just judgment God does not withhold his mercy from good minds in any nation, while allowing no nobility of ancestry to defend evil minds. The Jews should understand that they must not despise the nations' faith. Just as Israelite ancestry does not defend crimes, so Gentile descent is no obstacle to virtues. The apostle pursues all this in that debate. In some passages, however, to bow down the pride of the circumcised, he settles the issue on God's power alone under the name of grace (Genesis 25:29–34) (Genesis 27:34–38) (Genesis 25:27) (Genesis 27:8).
